lesson.title: Zählen I: eins, vier, fünf, sechs, zehn
lesson.subtitle: the everyday count — and the T→S shift hiding inside zehn

hook.title: Five Numbers, Three Shift Families
hook.content: You already own drei, zwei and hundert. These five fill the gaps you actually use — and they arrive wearing three different shift badges. zehn is the T→S family: German zehn and English ten are the same sound with the T hardened to a Z-sound, exactly like zwei/two and Zahn/tooth. drei is the opposite badge, TH→D: German hardened the þ to d (drei), while English kept the breathy th sound and changed only the letter (three). eins has no badge at all: German eins and English one both fall back to Proto-Germanic *ainaz, the very first number any Indo-European language ever had. fünf and sechs are the plain ones — sound twins with no shift, which is precisely why they are easy. The number system is not a chore. It is the shift atlas with the volume turned up.

footnotes.title: Why the Clock Is a Number Lesson
footnotes.content: Es ist fünf Uhr — 'it is five o'clock' — is the sentence Germans say more often than any other time sentence. The number, the noun Uhr and sein: three items, all drilled today. Say it wrong and you are understood; say it right and you are understood faster.

pattern.title: Where the Number Stands
pattern.content: Three frames, one rule. 1. With sein: Es ist fünf Uhr (it is five o'clock) — the number simply stands in for the subject. 2. Counting: Ich zähle bis zehn (I count to ten) — zählen takes an endpoint, bis marks the ceiling. 3. With a noun: Ich habe vier Bücher (I have four books) — the number sits in front and the plural noun follows it bare, with NO article: nicht vier Bücher but vier Bücher. The clock: Es ist zwölf Uhr / Es ist sechs Uhr morgens. And the promise: Ich warte zehn Minuten (I wait ten minutes) — accusative time, no preposition.
pattern.linguist_note: The bare plural after a numeral is old: Latin, Greek and English all once said 'four oxen'. English kept the bare noun only after a few dozen ('four hundred men'); German never raised the threshold, so *vier Bücher* still sounds as natural as *four books*.

exercises.prompt: The everyday count — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: I have only one of those

exercises.target_answer: Ich zähle bis zehn, Es ist fünf Uhr, Es ist zwölf Uhr, Ich habe nur eins davon, Ich habe vier Bücher, Ich warte zehn Minuten
exercises.meaning: counting, telling the time, counting things, waiting
exercises.explanation: Five numbers in six frames. The bare plural after the numeral (vier Bücher, no article) is the German reflex of an older English 'four books'; the accusative Minute takes no preposition at all.

exercises.prompt: Which of these numbers wears the T→S shift badge (as in zwei→two)?
exercises.meaning: zehn ↔ ten: the T→S/SS shift family
exercises.explanation: zehn is the T→S family: the ancient T hardened to a Z-sound, and English kept the soft T in ten. vier and sechs shifted in neither direction (pure sound twins); eins has no shift — it is Proto-Germanic *ainaz, the first number.

exercises.prompt: 'drei' wears the TH→D badge: German hardened the th to d. Which English word is its twin?
exercises.meaning: drei ↔ three: the TH→D family runs the other way from T→S
exercises.explanation: Both languages start from Proto-Germanic *þrīz. German hardened the þ to d; English kept the breathy th and later dropped it. Same ancient numeral, two sound laws pulling in opposite directions.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the time sentence: 'It is five o'clock'
exercises.explanation: es + ist + the number + die Uhr. The impersonal es does the work no German sentence ever asks a person to do.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the counting sentence: 'I count to ten'

vocab_hints.note: bis marks the ceiling of a count — Ich zähle bis zehn, not bis elf. English 'to' here is not 'until'.

exercises.explanation: zählen takes an endpoint; bis tells you where the counting stops. hundert sits in the bank to prove the frame scales: Ich zähle bis hundert.

summary.outcome: Count, tell the time, and put a bare plural after a number without thinking about it.

use_example.german: Es ist fünf Uhr — ich zähle bis zehn.
use_example.english: It is five o'clock — I count to ten.

summary.takeaway: zehn wears the T→S badge, drei wears TH→D, eins is the untouched original — and vier Bücher takes no article.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: null and the nouns that count for you — die Zahl, die Nummer, die Hälfte, die Million.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Zählen I: eins, vier, fünf, sechs, zehn (I count to ten):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich zähle bis zehn" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Zählen I: eins, vier, fünf, sechs, zehn without relying on short-term echo.

eins.context_translation: I have only one of those.
eins.etymology_derivation: Contraction of eines, Proto-Germanic *ainaz — the twin of English one (see ein). [wiktionary]

vier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *feuwar — the direct twin of English four. [wiktionary]

fünf.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fimf, PIE *pénkʷe — the twin of English five. [wiktionary]

sechs.context_translation: It is six o'clock in the morning.
sechs.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *sehs, PIE *swéḱs — the same root as English six. [wiktionary]

zehn.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *tehun — the twin of English ten with the classic t → z shift. [wiktionary]

zählen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *taljaną, the causative of the tal-root — the same family as English tell and tale; the initial t became z, as in two, zwei. [wiktionary]

hundert.context_phrase: Ein Jahr hat nicht hundert Tage.
hundert.context_translation: A year does not have a hundred days.
hundert.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaradą 'hundred-count' — the twin of English hundred. [wiktionary]

zwölf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twalif — 'two left over', the exact tw → zw twin of twelve. [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

zeichen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
zeichen.context_translation: That is a good sign / token.
zeichen.etymology_derivation: Double shift: t → z and k → ch (token ↔ Zeichen).

mineralwasser.context_translation: I am drinking a cold mineral water.
mineralwasser.etymology_derivation: Compound of Mineral and Wasser; Mineral matches English mineral, a Latin loan, and Wasser corresponds to English water via the t to ss shift. [wiktionary]

knien.context_translation: He kneels next to the child.
knien.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Middle High German kniewen, by surface analysis Knie plus -en. English knee continues the same Proto-Germanic noun. [wiktionary]

direktor.context_translation: The principal works in the office.
direktor.etymology_derivation: From Latin director, the agent noun of dirigere (to guide straight); English director is from the same Latin verb. [wiktionary][etymonline]

zeichnen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
zeichnen.etymology_derivation: From Zeichen (sign, token) - compare English token: the same old word shifted by t-to-z and k-to-ch, like two-zwei and make-machen. [wiktionary]

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Described by Walter Skeat as the primary dental affrication and spirantization of High German.
